newsitem.title: USA: US Feb imports surge, may dent Q1 GDP estimates.
newsitem.headline: US Feb imports surge, may dent Q1 GDP estimates.

text.p: Surprising strength in imports boosted the U.S. international trade deficit above Wall Street expectations and could spur analysts to trim their gross domestic product (GDP) forecasts for the first quarter.

"It's a larger deficit than we expected mainly because imports, rather than declining slightly or holding steady as we expected, made a strong upward surge consistent with the strength in domestic demand," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
"The impact of this on GDP estimates will probably be to lower peoples' estimates," he added.

The Commerce Department reported on Thursday that the overall U.S. trade deficit in goods and services in February fell 8.5 percent to $11.59 billion, narrowing less than the $10.1 billion gap economists had forecast according to a Reuters poll.
January's ballooning deficit, which hit a near-decade high, was downwardly revised to a $12.67 billion shortfall from a previously reported $12.71 billion gap.
Economists attributed the larger-than-expected deficit, in part, to strong U.S. domestic demand "sucking in" imports.

"This is a symptom of our success. If you have an economy which is growing close to 5.0 percent in real terms in the first quarter, you're going to get a huge surge in imports," said David Kelly, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.
"It doesn't mean there's anything wrong in your export sector," he added.
In fact, exports grew a healthy 4.0 percent in February, counterbalanced by a 2.1 percent gain in imports.

While the trade deficit probably detracted from first quarter GDP, strong demand most likely kept GDP growth over 3.5 percent, said Sally Kleinman, economist at Chase Securities Inc. U.S. GDP grew at 3.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.

"...The U.S. economy is hot and we're sucking up a lot of imports...This may slice just a little bit off of the GDP numbers for the first quarter," said Joseph Dziwura, vice president and economist at The Sakura Bank, Ltd.

The February gains in imports and exports, for the most part, were evenly distributed across the major categories except for an increase in crude oil imports and a jump in aircraft exports, said Sandy Batten, international economist at Citicorp.
Financial market reaction to the data was minimal. The dollar weakened slightly against the mark and yen immediately following the report, while U.S. Treasuries shrugged off the news.
Dollar/yen was mostly unaffected by the slight narrowing of the U.S. bilateral deficit with Japan to $4.255 billion from $4.294 billion.
